structure.overview: The case concerns the judicial review of a refusal by an immigration officer to grant humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) relief to the Applicants, who sought to extend their visitor status in Canada. The Applicants challenged the Officer's decision, arguing it was unreasonable due to errors in assessing their establishment in Canada, family ties, and hardship factors. The Federal Court granted the judicial review, finding the Officer's decision unreasonable due to factual and logical errors.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court grants the Application for judicial review.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicants' visitor status in Canada was extended repeatedly until October 11, 2023, when their visitor records expired.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On December 9, 2022, the Applicants submitted their H&C application with required forms, ID, and submissions addressing relevant criteria and hardship factors.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On March 4, 2024, the Officer refused the Applicants' H&C application, finding no exemption justified and no undue hardship on return to India.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer gave little weight to Applicants' establishment in Canada, finding limited community involvement and that 1.5 years was too short to be established.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer gave some weight to family ties but discounted evidence of living in Greece, focusing on India and concluding minimal hardship on return.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer gave little weight to health hardship claims, citing lack of evidence and noting Applicants' good physical health and available communication methods.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer gave little weight to best interests of the grandchild, noting possible future visits, child's adaptability, and parental care.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer gave little weight to adverse country conditions in India, noting lack of personal incidents and police action against crimes, and that such crimes occur in Canada too.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer rejected the H&C application, finding insufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations on a global assessment.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On March 12, 2024, the Applicants sought judicial review of the Officer's Decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The general rule restricts judicial review evidence to that before the decision maker, with exceptions for background, procedural defects, or absence of evidence, citing Access Copyright.

citations.cite: Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency (Access Copyright), 2012 FCA 22 at paras 19-20
citations.why: States rule on admissibility of new evidence on judicial review

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent submits none of the exceptions apply to the new evidence; the Applicants only argue it shows unreasonableness, which the court rejects.

citations.cite: Farah v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 503 at para 60
citations.why: Respondent cites to support exceptions list is not closed

citations.cite: Perez v Hull, 2019 FCA 238 at paras 16-17
citations.why: Court cites to explain roles of reviewing court and decision maker

citations.cite: Bernard v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2015 FCA 263 at para 28
citations.why: Court cites to explain roles of reviewing court and decision maker
Court cites to explain roles of reviewing court and decision maker

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Four of the Further Affidavits and exhibits A-G of the Principal Applicant's affidavit go to merits and do not fall under exceptions, so cannot be admitted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Principal Applicant's remaining affidavit contains new evidence post-refusal going to merits, including exhibits B, C, D, E, F, and G, which cannot be admitted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Exhibits H and I were previously submitted to the Officer and thus are not new evidence and can be admitted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Paragraphs 10-20 of the Principal Applicant's affidavit contain impermissible argument and opinion and are disregarded as inadmissible under Rule 81.

citations.cite: Canada (Attorney General) v Quadrini, 2010 FCA 47 at para 18
citations.why: Affidavits must be confined to facts without argument or opinion

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness review requires assessing justification, transparency, and intelligibility, considering the decision's rationale and coherence, citing Vavilov and Pepa.

citations.why: Defines hallmarks of reasonableness

citations.cite: Pepa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 SCC 21 at para 51
citations.why: Defines hallmarks of reasonableness
Court must consider outcome with rationale
Decision must be coherent and justified
Decision must be coherent and justified
Applicant bears onus to show unreasonableness
Unreasonableness includes failure of rationality or justification
Unreasonableness includes failure of rationality or justification

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 25(1) grants discretion to exempt foreign nationals based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations, per Kanthasamy.

citations.cite: Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 31-33
citations.why: Explains discretionary nature of H&C relief

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Discretion must align with H&C considerations, assessed globally, per Kanthasamy, Kapoor, Baker, and Chirwa.

citations.cite: Kapoor v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 2095 at para 41
citations.why: Discretion must be consistent with H&C considerations
Discretion must be consistent with H&C considerations
Discretion must be consistent with H&C considerations
Endorses Chirwa approach to H&C considerations

citations.cite: Chirwa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1970), 4 IAC 338
citations.why: Defines H&C considerations as facts evoking desire to relieve misfortunes
Quotes Chirwa on H&C considerations
Requires global assessment of all relevant facts

citations.cite: Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paras 74-75
citations.why: Requires weighing all relevant facts in H&C assessment

citations.cite: Semana v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1082 at para 15
citations.why: H&C relief is exceptional and discretionary

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicants argue the Officer failed to conduct a thorough global analysis; court limits analysis to four main reasons for unreasonableness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer's misapprehension of time in Canada is a reviewable error affecting the Establishment finding.

citations.cite: Isaac Johnson v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 1364 at para 14
citations.why: Failure to address contradictory evidence is reviewable error

citations.cite: Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1998 CanLII 8667 (FC) at para 16
citations.why: Officers presumed to consider all evidence but failure to address key evidence is error

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The misapprehension of evidence impacts the global analysis; establishment alone rarely suffices for H&C relief but error remains significant.

citations.cite: Ntsima v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1254 at para 11
citations.why: Establishment alone rarely justifies H&C relief

citations.cite: Zlotosz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 724 at para 35
citations.why: Establishment alone rarely justifies H&C relief

citations.cite: Herrera v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 261 at para 20
citations.why: Establishment alone rarely justifies H&C relief
Global analysis required in H&C assessment
Global analysis required in H&C assessment

citations.cite: Salde v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 386 at para 27
citations.why: Misapprehension impacts global analysis

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer confined consideration of family ties to India alone, ignoring Greece.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Evidence shows Applicants lived in Greece for many years before Canada, contradicting Officer's belief of little evidence of Greek residence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer's belief that Applicants lived about 60 years in India is inaccurate and puzzling given their ages and time in Greece.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Ignoring Applicants' time in Greece, the Officer failed to consider its impact on family ties in India, constituting a reviewable error.

citations.why: Failure to consider relevant evidence is reviewable error

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer reasonably required evidence of personal victimization, but the Officer's assessment was less nuanced and unreasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer failed to apply the Chirwa standard and consider all evidence as required by Kanthasamy and Baker, making the decision unreasonable.

citations.why: Decision must respect factual and legal constraints and consider relevant evidence

citations.cite: Federal Courts Act, RSC 1985, c F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)
citations.why: Court's power to review administrative decisions for reasonableness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the decision unreasonable due to factual and logical errors, citing Vavilov and Pepa to support losing confidence in the outcome.

citations.why: supports losing confidence in the decision due to errors
supports losing confidence in the decision due to errors

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees no question for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the Act arises as none was proposed by the parties.
